subject: Archaeology
title: Sumerian Mathematics
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Sumerian Mathematics.

hook.text: Sumerians invented a number system based on 60. That is why you have 60 seconds in a minute and 360 degrees in a circle.

buildup.text: Thousands of clay math tablets survive. Students practiced multiplication, division, square roots, and geometry.

discovery.text: Tablet YBC 7289 from 1800 BCE shows an accurate calculation of the square root of 2 — correct to six decimal places.

twist.text: Plimpton 322, a Babylonian tablet, contains Pythagorean triples — 1,000 years before Pythagoras was born.

climax.text: Mesopotamian math was practical: land measurement, trade accounts, and architectural planning drove innovation.

punchline.text: They invented the 60-second minute to manage irrigation.

quiz.question: What does the Plimpton 322 tablet demonstrate?
options: The oldest known star chart for astronomical observation
Pythagorean triples calculated 1,000 years before Pythagoras
The first known use of zero in mathematical calculations

details.summary: Sumerians developed a base-60 number system still embedded in our 60-minute hours and 360-degree circles. Their mathematical tablets show advanced arithmetic, geometry, and even early algebra used for land measurement, trade calculations, and astronomical observations.
details.whyItMatters: Sumerian math shaped the systems we still use today. Understanding their numerical achievements reveals that abstract mathematical thinking is as old as civilization itself.
takeaways: Sumerians used a base-60 system still reflected in modern timekeeping
Clay tablets show arithmetic, geometry, and early algebra
Mathematics served practical needs like land surveys and trade

faq.question: Why did the Sumerians use base-60 instead of base-10?
faq.answer: Base-60 is highly divisible — it divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20, and 30. This made fractions much easier to work with than in base-10, a practical advantage for trade calculations, dividing land, and astronomical observations.

faq.question: What mathematical achievements did the Sumerians make?
faq.answer: They calculated square roots, solved quadratic equations, and understood the Pythagorean theorem over a thousand years before Pythagoras. The Plimpton 322 tablet from around 1800 BCE contains a table of Pythagorean triples that amazed modern mathematicians.
